title: Sparks from one fire
hookLine: Angiras shows Shaunaka a blazing fire: every being is a spark of the one fire, and goes back to it
carry: every being is a spark of the one fire
tomorrow: the bow, the arrow, the target
last: COME TO THE GURU WITH FUEL IN HAND.

lines: A BONFIRE ON A COLD NIGHT.
EACH ONE IS THE SAME FIRE.
cards: A bonfire on a cold night. Someone drops on another log, and the fire answers with a fountain of sparks, hundreds of them, into the dark. Each one glows for a second, drifts, and fades.
Each one is small. And each one, while it lasts, is exactly what the fire is: the same heat, the same light, the same color. Nobody watching says, look, a different thing just left the fire.
The student has arrived with fuel. And the Mundaka's second chapter begins by pointing straight at the fire.

teach.b: Angiras goes on, and his second chapter opens: this is the truth.

As from a blazing fire sparks of the same form fly out by the thousands, so from the imperishable, dear one, beings of every kind are born, and to it they go back. Three things are packed into that picture.
First, there are many: thousands of sparks, every kind of being. You, your neighbor, the sparrow outside.
Second, they're sarupa, of the same form. A spark isn't a cheap copy of fire. It's fire, small.
Tatra chaivapiyanti: and there they return. The sparks rise from the fire and go back into it. Then the text describes the source.
The person, purusha, is divine and formless, outside and inside. Unborn. Without breath, without mind, pure.

From that, breath, mind, the senses, space, wind, light, water and the earth that holds everything are born. Then it draws that person as the whole cosmos, with the sun and moon for eyes and the earth from his feet.
The schools of Vedanta read the spark differently. Some hear identity: the spark is the fire. Others hear kinship: the soul shares the nature of God, and stays itself.
Both keep the fire, and the way home.

teach.h: ATMAN SHARES THE NATURE OF BRAHMAN.
teach.b: And both keep one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the atman, the self in every being, shares the nature of Brahman.
That includes the person you find hardest. Before you write anyone off, the spark picture asks: what fire did this one come from?

how: In Hindu homes and temples a lamp or flame is waved before the deity in arati, and some teachers use the sparks of Mundaka 2.1.1 to explain how each being shares in the divine.

o: the ash a fire leaves after it dies
a lamp waved before the deity in worship
a spark, of the same form as its fire

games.q: the sparks and the fire — tap the pairs.

s: in the verse, the sparks are a different stuff from the fire
they're sarupa, of the same form: fire, small.
the text says beings go back to the imperishable
as sparks rise from the fire, and to it they return.
the Mundaka describes the person as formless, without breath or mind
divine, formless, unborn, pure, and outside and inside.

games.q: thousands of sparks fly up from the fire. in the Mundaka, what happens to them?
o: they're lost forever in the dark.
each becomes a new, separate fire.
games.why: tatra chaivapiyanti: and there they return. beings come from the imperishable and go back to it.

practice: Fold your hands at your chest, the way many Hindus greet each other, and feel the warmth of your own palms: your spark, small, bright, real.
Then picture someone you'll see today, someone easy, then someone hard, and bow to each in your mind: many sparks, one fire. If folded hands aren't your way, just hold each face for one breath.

wordCard.voice: Visphulinga, a spark. The Mundaka's picture: as thousands of sparks of the same form fly from a blazing fire, so beings come from the imperishable, and return.

orig.note: Sanskrit visphuliṅga, spark: 'from a blazing fire, sparks by the thousands', Mundaka 2.1.1.
